entries.1c883ce588c4ebb7d848d1f16365abce073d0906: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv24"/><title type="x-ms">Job to Song of Solomon</title> <div sID="gen9133" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen9133" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9134" type="x-p"/> <hi type="small-caps">These</hi> five books of scripture which are contained in this third volume and which I have here endeavoured, according to the measure of the gift given to me, to explain and improve, for the use of those who desire to read them, not only with understanding, but to their edification—though they have the same divine origin, design, and authority, as those that went before, yet, upon some accounts, are of a very different nature from them, and from the rest of the sacred writings, such variety of methods has Infinite Wisdom seen fit to take in conveying the light of divine revelation to the children of men, that this heavenly food might have (as the Jews say of the manna) something in it agreeable to every palate and suited to every constitution. If every eye be not thus opened, every mouth will be stopped, and such as perish in their ignorance will be left without excuse. <hi type="italic">We have piped unto you, and you have not danced, we have mourned unto you, and you have not lamented,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.11.17">Matt. xi. 17</reference>. <div eID="gen9134" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9135" type="x-p"/> I. The books of scripture have hitherto been, for the most part, very plain and easy, narratives of matter of fact, which he that runs may read and understand, and which are milk for babes, such as they can receive and digest, and both entertain and nourish themselves with. The waters of the sanctuary have hitherto been but to the ankles or to the knees, such as a lamb might wade in, to drink of and wash in; but here we are advanced to a higher form in God's school, and have books put into our hands wherein are <hi type="italic">many things dark and hard to be understood,</hi> which we do not apprehend the meaning of so suddenly and so certainly as we could wish, the study of which requires a more close application of mind, a greater intenseness of thought, and the accomplishing of a diligent search, which yet the treasure hid in them, when it is found, will abundantly recompense. The waters of the sanctuary are here <hi type="italic">to the loins,</hi> and still as we go forward we shall find the waters still risen in the prophetical books, <hi type="italic">waters to swim in</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ezek.47.3-Ezek.47.5">Ezek. xlvii. 3-5</reference>), not fordable, nor otherwise to be passed over—depths in which an elephant will not find footing, <hi type="italic">strong meat for strong men.</hi> The same method is observable in the New Testament, where we find the plain history of Christ and his gospel placed first in the Evangelists and the Acts of the Apostles; then the mystery of both in the Epistles, which are more difficult to be understood; and, lastly, the prophesies of things to come in the apocalyptic visions. This method, so exactly observed in both the Testaments, directs us in what order to proceed both in studying the things of God ourselves and in teaching them to others; we must go in the order that the scripture does; and where can we expect to find a better method of divinity and a better method of preaching? <div eID="gen9135" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9136" type="x-p"/> 1. We must begin with those things that are most plain and easy, as, blessed be God, those things are which are most necessary to salvation and of the greatest use. We must lay our foundation firm, in a sound experimental knowledge of the principles of religion, and then the super-structure will be well reared and will stand firmly. It is not safe to launch out into the deep at first, nor to venture into points difficult and controverted until we have first thoroughly digested the elements of the oracles of God and turned them <hi type="italic">in succum et sanguinem—into juice and blood.</hi> Those that begin their Bible at the wrong end commonly use their knowledge of it in the wrong way. And, in training up others, we must be sure to ground them well at first in those truths of God which are plain, and in some measure level to their capacity, which we find they comprehend, and relish, and know how to make use of, and not amuse those that are weak with things above them, things of doubtful disputation, which they cannot apprehend any certainty of nor advantage by. Our Lord Jesus spoke the word to the people <hi type="italic">as they were able to hear it</hi> (<reference osisRef="Mark.4.33">Mark iv. 33</reference>) and had many things to say to his disciples which he did not say because as yet they <hi type="italic">could not bear them,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.16.12-John.16.13">John xvi. 12, 13</reference>. And those whom St. Paul <hi type="italic">could not speak to as unto spiritual</hi>—though he blamed them for their backwardness, yet he accommodated himself to their weakness, and spoke to them <hi type="italic">as unto babes in Christ,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Cor.3.1-1Cor.3.2">1 Cor. iii. 1, 2</reference>. <div eID="gen9136" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9137" type="x-p"/> 2. Yet we must not rest in these things. We must not be always children that have need of milk, but nourished up with that, and gaining strength, we must <hi type="italic">go on to perfection</hi> (<reference osisRef="Heb.6.1">Heb. vi. 1</reference>), that having, <hi type="italic">by reason of use, our spiritual senses exercised</hi> (<reference osisRef="Heb.5.14">Heb. v. 14</reference>), we may come to full age, and put away childish things, and, <hi type="italic">forgetting the things which are behind,</hi> that is, so well remembering them (<reference osisRef="Phil.3.13">Phil. iii. 13</reference>) that we need not be still poring over them as those that are ever learning the same lesson, we may reach forth to the things which are before. Though we must never think to learn above our Bible, as long as we are here in this world, yet we must still be getting forward in it. <hi type="italic">You have dwelt long enough in this mountain;</hi> now turn and take your journey onward in the wilderness towards Canaan. Our motto must be <hi type="italic">Plus ultra—Onward.</hi> And then shall we know if thus, by regular steps (<reference osisRef="Hos.6.3">Hos. vi. 3</reference>), we <hi type="italic">follow on to know the Lord</hi> and what the mind of the Lord is. <div eID="gen9137" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9138" type="x-p"/> II. The books of scripture have hitherto been mostly historical, but now the matter is of another nature; it is doctrinal and devotional, preaching and praying; and in this way of writing, as well as in the former, a great deal of excellent knowledge is conveyed, which serves very valuable purposes. It will be of good use to know not only what others did that went before us, and how they fared, but what their notions and sentiments were, what their thoughts and affections were, that we may, with the help of them, form our minds aright. Plutarch's Morals are reputed as a useful treasure in the commonwealth of learning as Plutarch's Lives, and the wise disquisitions and discourses of the philosophers as the records of the historians; nor is this divine philosophy (if I may so call it), which we have in these books, less needful, nor less serviceable, to the church, than the sacred history was. Blessed be God for both. <div eID="gen9138" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9139" type="x-p"/> III. The Jews make these books to be given by a divine inspiration somewhat different from that both of Moses and the prophets. They divided the books of the Old Testament into the Law, the Prophets and the <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">ktwbym</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">Writings,</hi> which Epiphanius emphatically translates <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">grapheia</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">things written,</hi> and these books are more commonly called among the Greeks <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">Hagiographa</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">Holy writings:</hi> the Jews attribute them to that distinct kind of inspiration which they call <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">rwh hqds</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">The Holy Spirit.</hi> Moses they supposed to write by the Spirit in a way above all the other prophets, for <hi type="italic">with him</hi> God spoke <hi type="italic">mouth to mouth, even apparently</hi> (<reference osisRef="Num.12.8">Num. xii. 8</reference>) <hi type="italic">knew him,</hi> that is, conversed with him <hi type="italic">face to face,</hi> <reference osisRef="Deut.34.10">Deut. xxxiv. 10</reference>. He was made partaker of divine revelation (as Maimonides distinguishes, <hi type="italic">De Fund. Legis, c.</hi> 7) <hi type="italic">per vigiliam—while awake,</hi><note placement="foot">See Mr. Smith's Discourses on Prophecy, c. 11.</note> whereas God manifested himself to all the other prophets in a dream or vision: and he adds that Moses understood the words of prophecy without any perturbation or astonishment of mind, whereas the other prophets commonly fainted and were troubled. But the writers of the Hagiographa they suppose to be inspired in a degree somewhat below that of the other prophets, and to receive divine revelation, not as they did by dreams, and visions, and voices, but (as Maimonides describes it, <hi type="italic">More Nevochim—part</hi> 2 <hi type="italic">c.</hi> 45) they perceived some power to rise within them, and rest upon them, which urged and enabled them to write or speak far above their own natural ability, in psalms or hymns, or in history or in rules of good living, still enjoying the ordinary vigour and use of their senses. Let David himself describe it. <hi type="italic">The Spirit of the Lord spoke by me, and his word was in my tongue; the God of Israel said, the Rock of Israel spoke to me,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Sam.23.2-2Sam.23.3">2 Sam. xxiii. 2, 3</reference>. This gives such a magnificent account of the inspiration by which David wrote that I see not why it should be made inferior to that of the other prophets, for David is expressly called <hi type="italic">a prophet,</hi> <reference osisRef="Acts.2.29-Acts.2.30">Acts ii. 29, 30</reference>. But, since our hand is in with the Jewish masters, let us see what books they account Hagiographa. These five that are now before us come, without dispute, into this rank of sacred writers, and the book of the Lamentations is not unfitly added to them. Indeed the Jews, when they would speak critically, reckon all those songs which we meet with in the Old Testament among the Hagiographa; for though they were penned by prophets, and under the direction of the Holy Ghost, yet, because they were not the proper result of a <hi type="italic">visum propheticum—prophetic vision,</hi> they were not strictly prophecy. As to the historical books, they distinguish (but I think it is a distinction without a difference); some of them they assign to the prophets, calling them the <hi type="italic">prophetæ priores—the former prophets,</hi> namely, Joshua, Judges, and the two books of the Kings; but others they rank among the Hagiographa, as the book of Ruth (which yet is but an appendix to the book of Judges), the two books of Chronicles, with Ezra, Nehemiah, and the book of Esther, which last the rabbin have a great value for, and think it is to be had in equal esteem with the law of Moses itself, that it shall last as long as that lasts, and shall survive the writings of the Prophets. And, <hi type="italic">lastly,</hi> they reckon the book of Daniel among the Hagiographa,<note placement="foot">Hil. Megil. c. 2, &#167; 11.</note> for which no reason can be given, since he was not inferior to any of the prophets in the gift of prophecy; and therefore the learned Mr. Smith thinks that their placing him among the Hagiographical writers was fortuitous by mistake.<note placement="foot">Vid. Hottinger. Thesaur. lib. 2, cap. 1, &#167; 3.</note> Mr. Smith, in his Discourse before quoted, though he supposes this kind of divine inspiration to be more "<hi type="italic">pacate</hi> and <hi type="italic">serene</hi> than that which was strictly called <hi type="italic">prophecy,</hi> not acting so much upon the imagination, but seating itself in the higher and purer faculties of the soul, yet shows that it manifested itself to be of a divine nature, not only as it always elevated pious souls into strains of devotion, or moved them strangely to dictate matters of true piety and goodness, but as it came in abruptly upon the minds of those holy men, and transported them from the temper of mind they were in before, so that they perceived themselves captivated by the power of some higher light than that which their own understanding commonly poured out upon them; and this, says he, was a kind of vital form to that light of divine and sanctified reason which they were perpetually possessed of and that constant frame of holiness and goodness which dwelt in their hallowed minds." We have reason to <hi type="italic">glorify the God of Israel who gave such power unto men</hi> and has here transmitted to us the blessed products of that power. <div eID="gen9139" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9140" type="x-p"/> IV. The style and composition of these books are different from those that go before and those that follow. Our Saviour divides the books of the Old Testament into <hi type="italic">the Law, the Prophets,</hi> and <hi type="italic">the Psalms</hi> (<reference osisRef="Luke.24.44">Luke xxiv. 44</reference>), and thereby teaches us to distinguish those books that are poetical, or metrical, from the Law and the Prophets; and such are all these that are now before us, except Ecclesiastes, which yet, having something restrained in its style, may well enough be reckoned among them. They are books in verse, according to the ancient rules of versifying, though not according to the Greek and Latin <hi type="italic">prosodies.</hi> Some of the ancients call these five books <hi type="italic">the second Pentateuch of the Old Testament,</hi><note placement="foot">Damascen. Orthod. Fid. l. 4, cap. 18.</note> five sacred volumes which are as the satellites to the five books of the law of Moses. <hi type="italic">Gregory Nazianzen</hi><note placement="foot">Vid. Suicer. Thesaur. in <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">stichera.</hi></hi></note> (<hi type="italic">carm.</hi> 33, <hi type="italic">p.</hi> 98) calls these <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">hai sticherai pente</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">the five metrical books;</hi> first Job (so he reckons them up), then David, then the three of Solomon-Ecclesiastes, the Song, and Proverbs. <hi type="italic">Amphilochius,</hi> bishop at Iconium, in his iambic poem to <hi type="italic">Seleucus,</hi> reckons them up particularly, and calls them <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">sticheras pente Biblos</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">the five verse-books. Epiphanius</hi> (<hi type="italic">lib. de ponder. et mensur. p.</hi> 533) <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">pente stichereis</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">the five verse-books.</hi> And <hi type="italic">Cyril. Hierosol. Collect.</hi> 4, <hi type="italic">p.</hi> 30 (<hi type="italic">mihi—in my copy</hi>), calls these five books <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">ta stichera</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">books in verse.</hi> Polychronius, in his prologue to Job, says that as <hi type="italic">those that are without</hi> call their tragedies and comedies <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">poietika</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">poetics,</hi> so, in sacred writ, those books which are composed in Hebrew metre (of which he reckons Job the first) we call <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">stichera biblia</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">books in verse,</hi> written <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">kata stichon</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">according to order.</hi> What is written in metre, or rhythm, is so called from <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">metros</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">a measure,</hi> and <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">arithmos</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">a number,</hi> because regulated by certain measures, or numbers of syllables, which please the ear with their smoothness and cadency, and so insinuate the matter the more movingly and powerfully into the fancy. Sir William Temple,<note placement="foot">Miscell, part 2.</note> in his essay upon poetry, thinks it is generally agreed to have been the first sort of writing that was used in the world, nay, that, in several nations, poetical compositions preceded the very invention or usage of letters. The Spaniards (he says) found in America many strains of poetry, and such as seemed to flow from a true poetic vein, before any letters were known in those regions. The same (says he) is probable of the Scythians and Grecians: the oracles of Apollo were delivered in verse. Homer and Hesiod wrote their poems (the very Alcoran of the pagan dæmonology) many ages before the appearing of any of the Greek philosophers or historians; and long before them (if we may give credit to the antiquities of Greece), even before the days of David, Orpheus and Linus were celebrated poets and musicians in Greece; and at the same time Carmenta, the mother of Evander, who was the first that introduced letters among the natives of Greece, was so called <hi type="italic">&#224; carmine—from a song,</hi> because she expressed herself in verse. And in such veneration was this way of writing among the ancients that their poets were called <hi type="italic">vates—prophets,</hi> and their muses were deified. But, which is more certain and considerable, the most ancient composition that we meet with in scripture was the song of Moses at the Red Sea (<reference osisRef="Exod.15.1-Exod.15.27">Exod. xv.</reference>), which we find before the very first mention of writing, for that occurs not until <reference osisRef="Exod.17.14">Exod. xvii. 14</reference>, when God bade Moses write a memorial of the war with Amalek. The first, and indeed the true and general end of writing, is a help of memory; and poetry does in some measure answer that end, and even in the want of writing, much more with writing, helps to preserve the remembrance of ancient things. The book of <hi type="italic">the wars of the Lord</hi> (<reference osisRef="Num.21.14">Num. xxi. 14</reference>), and the book of Jasher (<reference osisRef="Josh.10.13">Josh. x. 13</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Sam.1.18">2 Sam. i. 18</reference>), seem to have been both written in poetic measures. Many sacred songs we meet with in the Old Testament, scattered both in the historical and prophetical books, penned on particular occasions, which, in the opinion of very competent judges, "have in them as true and noble strains of poetry and picture as are met with in any other language whatsoever, in spite of all disadvantages from translations into such different tongues and common prose,<note placement="foot">Sir W. Temple, p. 329.</note> nay, are nobler examples of the true sublime style of poetry than any that can be found in the Pagan writers; the images are so strong, the thoughts so great, the expressions so divine, and the figures so admirably bold and moving, that the wonderful manner of these writers is quite inimitable."<note placement="foot">Sir R. Blackmore's preface to Job.</note> It is fit that what is employed in the service of the sanctuary should be the best in its kind. <div eID="gen9140" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9141" type="x-p"/> The books here put together are poetical. Job is an heroic poem, the book of Psalms a collection of divine odes or lyrics, Solomon's Song a pastoral and an epithalamium; they are poetical, and yet sacred and serious, grave and full of majesty. They have a poetic force and flame, with out poetic fury and fiction, and strangely command and move the affections, without corrupting the imagination or putting a cheat upon it; and, while they gratify the ear, they edify the mind and profit the more by pleasing. It is therefore much to be lamented that so powerful an art, which was at first consecrated to the honour of God, and has been so often employed in his service, should be debauched, as it has been, and is at this day, into the service of his enemies—that his corn, and wine, and oil should be prepared for Baal. <div eID="gen9141" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9142" type="x-p"/> V. As the manner of the composition of these books is excellent, and very proper to engage the attention, move the affections, and fix them in the memory, so the matter is highly useful, and such as will be every way serviceable to us. They have in them the very sum and substance of religion, and what they contain is more fitted to our hand, and made ready for use, than any part of the Old Testament, upon which account, if we may be allowed to compare one star with another in the firmament of the scripture, these will be reckoned stars of the first magnitude. <hi type="italic">All scripture is profitable</hi> (and this part of it in a special manner) <hi type="italic">for instruction</hi> in doctrine, in devotion, and in the right ordering of the conversation. The book of Job directs us what we are to believe concerning God, the book of Psalms how we are to worship him, pay our homage to him, and maintain our communion with him, and then the book of the Proverbs shows very particularly how we are to govern ourselves <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">en pase anastrophe</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">in every turn of human life;</hi> thus shall the <hi type="italic">man of God,</hi> by a due attention to these lights, be <hi type="italic">perfect, thoroughly furnished for every good work.</hi> And these are placed according to their natural order, as well as according to the order of time; for very fitly are we first led into the knowledge of God, our judgments rightly formed concerning him, and our mistakes rectified, and then instructed how to worship him and to choose the things that please him. We have here much of natural religion, its principles, its precepts—much of God, his infinite perfections, his relations to man, and his government both of the world and of the church; here is much of Christ, who is the spring, and soul, and centre, of revealed religion, and whom both Job and David were eminent types of, and had clear and happy prospects of. We have here that which will be of use to enlighten our understandings, and to acquaint us more and more with the things of God, with the deep things of God—speculations to entertain the most contemplative, and discoveries to satisfy the most inquisitive and increase the knowledge of those that are most knowing. Here is that also which, with a divine light, will bring into the soul the heat and influence of a divine fire, will kindle and inflame pious and devout affections, on which wings we may soar upwards until we enter into the holiest. We may here be in the mount with God, to behold his beauty; and when we come down from that mount, if we retain (as we ought) the impressions of our devotion upon our spirits and make conscience of doing that good which the Lord our God here requires of us, our faces shall shine before all with whom we converse, who shall take occasion thence to <hi type="italic">glorify our Father who is in heaven,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.5.16">Matt. v. 16</reference>. Thus great, thus noble, thus truly excellent, is the subject, and thus capable of being improved, which gives me the more reason to be ashamed of the meanness of my performance, that the comment breathes so little of the life and spirit of the text. We often wonder at those that are not at all affected with the great things of God, and have no taste nor relish of them, because they know little of them; but perhaps we have more reason to wonder at ourselves, that conversing so frequently, so intimately, with them, we are not more affected with them, so as even to be wholly taken up with them, and in a continual transport of delight in the contemplation of them. We hope to be so shortly; in the mean time, though like the three disciples that were the witnesses of Christ's transfiguration upon the mount we are but dull and sleepy, yet we can say, <hi type="italic">Master, it is good to be here;</hi> here <hi type="italic">let us make tabernacles,</hi> <reference osisRef="Luke.9.32-Luke.9.33">Luke ix. 32, 33</reference>. <div eID="gen9142" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9143" type="x-p"/> I have nothing here to boast of—nothing at all, but a great deal to be humbled for, that I have not come up to what I have aimed at in respect of fulness and exactness. In the review of the work, I find many defects, and those who are critical, perhaps, will meet with some mistakes in it; but I have done it with what care I could, and desire to be thankful to God who by his grace has carried me on in his work thus far: let that grace have all the glory (<reference osisRef="Phil.2.13">Phil. ii. 13</reference>), which <hi type="italic">works in us both to will and to do</hi> whatever we will or do that is good or serves any good purpose. What is from God will, I trust, be to him, will be graciously accepted by him, <hi type="italic">according to what a man has, and not according to what he had not,</hi> and will be of some use to his church; and what is from myself (that is, all the defects and errors) will, I trust, be favourably passed by and pardoned. That prayer of <hi type="italic">St. Austin</hi> is mine, <hi type="italic">Domine Deus, quæcunque dixi in his libris de tuo, agnoscant et tui; et quæ de meo, et tu ignosce et tui—Lord God, whatever I have maintained in these books correspondent with what is contained in thine grant that thy people may approve as well as thyself; whatever is but the doctrine of my book forgive thou, and grant that thy people may forgive it also.</hi> I must beg likewise to own, to the honour of our great Master, that I have found the work to be its own wages, and that the more we converse with the word of God the more it is to us as <hi type="italic">the honey</hi> and the <hi type="italic">honeycomb,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.19.10">Ps. xix. 10</reference>. In gathering some gleaning of this harvest for others we may feast ourselves; and, when we are enabled by the grace of God to do so, we are best qualified to feed others. I was much pleased with a passage I lately met with of Erasmus, that great scholar and celebrated wit, in an epistle dedicatory before his book <hi type="italic">De Ratione Concionandi,</hi> where, as one weary of the world and the hurry of it, he expresses an earnest desire to spend the rest of his days in secret communion with Jesus Christ, encouraged by his gracious invitation to those who <hi type="italic">labour and are heavy laden</hi> to <hi type="italic">come unto him for rest</hi> (<reference osisRef="Matt.11.28">Matt. xi. 28</reference>), and this alone is that which he thinks will yield him true satisfaction. I think his words worth transcribing, and such as deserve to be inserted among the testimonies of great men to serious godliness. <hi type="italic">Neque quisquam facil&#232; credat qu&#224;m miser&#232; animus jamdudum affectet ab his laboribus in tranquillam otium secedere, quodque superest vitæ (superest autem vix brevis palmus sive pugillus), solum cum eo solo colloqui, qui clamavit olim (nec hodi&#232; mutat vocem suam), "Venite ad me, omnes qui laboratis et onerati estis, ego reficiam vos;" quandoquidem in tam turbulento, ne dicam furente, sæculo, in tot molestiis quas vel ipsa tempora public&#232; invehunt, vel privatim adfert oetas ac valetudo, nihil reperio in quo mens mea libentius conquiescat qu&#224;m in hoc arcano colloquio—No one will easily believe how anxiously, for a long time past, I have wished to retire from these labours into a scene of tranquility, and, during the remainder of life (dwindled, it is true, to the shortest span), to converse only with him who once cried (nor does he now retract), "Come unto me, all you that labour and are heavy laden, and I will refresh you," for in this turbulent, not to say furious, age, the many public sources of disquietude, connected with the infirmities of advancing age, leave no solace to my mind to be compared with this secret communion.</hi> In the pleasing contemplation of the divine beauty and benignity we hope to spend a blessed eternity, and therefore in this work it is good to spend as much as may be of our time. <div eID="gen9143" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9144" type="x-p"/> One volume more, containing the prophetical books, will finish the Old Testament, if the Lord continue my life, and leisure, and ability of mind and body for this work. It is begun, and I find it will be larger than any of the other volumes, and longer in the doing; but, as God by his grace shall furnish me for it and assist me in it (without which grace I am nothing, less than nothing, worse than nothing), it shall be carried on with all convenient speed; and <hi type="italic">sat cit&#242;, si sat ben&#232;—if with sufficient ability, it will be with sufficient speed.</hi> I desire the prayers of my friends that God would <hi type="italic">minister seed to the sower</hi> and <hi type="italic">bread to the eaters</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.55.10">Isa. lv. 10</reference>), that he would <hi type="italic">multiply the seed sown</hi> and <hi type="italic">increase the fruits of our righteousness</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Cor.9.10">2 Cor. ix. 10</reference>), that so he who <hi type="italic">sows and those who reap may rejoice together</hi> (<reference osisRef="John.4.36">John iv. 36</reference>); and the great Lord of the harvest shall have the glory of all. <div eID="gen9144" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9145" type="x-p"/> <hi type="small-caps">This</hi> book of Job stands by itself, is not connected with any other, and is therefore to be considered alone. Many copies of the Hebrew Bible place it after the book of Psalms, and some after the Proverbs, which perhaps has given occasion to some learned men to imagine it to have been written by Isaiah or some of the later prophets. But, as the subject appears to have been much more ancient, so we have no reason to think but that the composition of the book was, and that therefore it is most fitly placed first in this collection of divine morals: also, being doctrinal, it is proper to precede and introduce the book of Psalms, which is devotional, and the book of Proverbs, which is practical; for how shall we worship or obey a God whom we know not? As to this book, <div eID="gen9145" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9146" type="x-p"/> I. We are sure that it is given by inspiration of God, though we are not certain who was the penman of it. The Jews, though no friends to Job, because he was a stranger to the commonwealth of Israel, yet, as faithful conservators of <hi type="italic">the oracles of God</hi> committed to them, always retained this book in their sacred canon. The history is referred to by one apostle (<reference osisRef="Jas.5.11">James v. 11</reference>) and one passage (<reference osisRef="Job.5.13">ch. v. 13</reference>) is quoted by another apostle, with the usual form of quoting scripture, <hi type="italic">It is written,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Cor.3.19">1 Cor. iii. 19</reference>. It is the opinion of many of the ancients that this history was written by Moses himself in Midian, and delivered to his suffering brethren in Egypt, for their support and comfort under their burdens, and the encouragement of their hope that God would in due time deliver and enrich them, as he did this patient sufferer. Some conjecture that it was written originally in Arabic, and afterwards translated into Hebrew, for the use of the Jewish church, by Solomon (so Monsieur Jurieu) or some other inspired writer. It seems most probable to me that Elihu was the penman of it, at least of the discourses, because (<reference osisRef="Job.32.15-Job.32.16">ch. xxxii. 15, 16</reference>) he mingles the words of a historian with those of a disputant: but Moses perhaps wrote the first two chapters and the last, to give light to the discourses; for in them God is frequently called <hi type="italic">Jehovah,</hi> but not once in all the discourses, except <reference osisRef="Job.12.9">ch. xii. 9</reference>. That name was but little known to the patriarchs before Moses, <reference osisRef="Exod.6.3">Exod. vi. 3</reference>. If Job wrote it himself, some of the Jewish writers themselves own him a <hi type="italic">prophet among the Gentiles;</hi> if Elihu, we find he had a spirit of prophecy which <hi type="italic">filled him with matter and constrained him,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.32.18">ch. xxxii. 18</reference>. <div eID="gen9146" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9147" type="x-p"/> II. We are sure that it is, for the substance of it, a true history, and not a romance, though the dialogues are poetical. No doubt there was such a man as Job; the prophet Ezekiel names him with Noah and Daniel, <reference osisRef="Ezek.14.14">Ezek. xiv. 14</reference>. The narrative we have here of his prosperity and piety, his strange afflictions and exemplary patience, the substance of his conferences with his friends, and God's discourse with him out of the whirlwind, with his return at length to a very prosperous condition, no doubt is exactly true, though the inspired penman is allowed the usual liberty of putting the matter of which Job and his friends discoursed into his own words. <div eID="gen9147" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9148" type="x-p"/> III. We are sure that it is very ancient, though we cannot fix the precise time either when Job lived or when the book was written. So many, so evident, are its hoary hairs, the marks of its antiquity, that we have reason to think it of equal date with the book of Genesis itself, and that holy Job was contemporary with Isaac and Jacob; though not coheir with them of the promise of the earthly Canaan, yet a joint-expectant with them of the <hi type="italic">better country,</hi> that is, <hi type="italic">the heavenly.</hi> Probably he was of the posterity of Nahor, Abraham's brother, whose first-born was <hi type="italic">Uz</hi> (<reference osisRef="Gen.22.21">Gen. xxii. 21</reference>), and in whose family religion was for some ages kept up, as appears, <reference osisRef="Gen.31.53">Gen. xxxi. 53</reference>, where God is called, not only <hi type="italic">the God of Abraham,</hi> but <hi type="italic">the God of Nahor.</hi> He lived before the age of man was shortened to seventy or eighty, as it was in Moses's time, before sacrifices were confined to one altar, before the general apostasy of the nations from the knowledge and worship of the true God, and while yet there was no other idolatry known than the worship of the sun and moon, and that punished by the Judges, <reference osisRef="Job.31.26-Job.31.28">ch. xxxi. 26-28</reference>. He lived while God was known by the name of <hi type="italic">God Almighty</hi> more than by the name of <hi type="italic">Jehovah;</hi> for he is called <hi type="italic">Shaddai—the Almighty,</hi> above thirty times in this book. He lived while divine knowledge was conveyed, not by writing, but by tradition; for to that appeals are here made, <reference osisRef="Job.8.8">ch. viii. 8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.21.29">xxi. 29</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.15.18">xv. 18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.5.1">v. 1</reference>. And we have therefore reason to think that he lived before Moses, because here is no mention at all of the deliverance of Israel out of Egypt, or the giving of the law. There is indeed one passage which might be made to allude to the drowning of Pharaoh (<reference osisRef="Job.26.12">ch. xxvi. 12</reference>): <hi type="italic">He divideth the sea with his power, and by his understanding he smiteth through Rahab,</hi> which name Egypt is frequently called by in scripture, as <reference osisRef="Ps.87.4">Ps. lxxxvii. 4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.89.10">lxxxix. 10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.51.9">Isa. li. 9</reference>. But that may as well refer to the proud waves of the sea. We conclude therefore that we are here got back to the patriarchal age, and, besides its authority, we receive this book with veneration for its antiquity. <div eID="gen9148" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9149" type="x-p"/> IV. We are sure that it is of great use to the church, and to every good Christian, though there are many passages in it dark and hard to be understood. We cannot perhaps be confident of the true meaning of every Arabic word and phrase we meet with in it. It is a book that finds a great deal of work for the critics; but enough is plain to make the whole profitable, and it was all written for our learning. <div eID="gen9149" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9150" type="x-p"/> 1. This noble poem presents to us, in very clear and lively characters, these five things among others:—(1.) <hi type="italic">A monument of primitive theology.</hi> The first and great principles of the light of nature, on which natural religion is founded, are here, in a warm, and long, and learned dispute, not only taken for granted on all sides and not the least doubt made of them, but by common consent plainly laid down as eternal truths, illustrated and urged as affecting commanding truths. Were ever the being of God, his glorious attributes and perfections, his unsearchable wisdom, his irresistible power, his inconceivable glory, his inflexible justice, and his incontestable sovereignty, discoursed of with more clearness, fulness, reverence, and divine eloquence, than in this book? The creation of the world, and the government of it, are here admirably described, not as matters of nice speculation, but as laying most powerful obligations upon us to fear and serve, to submit to and trust in, our Creator, owner, Lord, and ruler. Moral good and evil, virtue and vice, were never drawn more to the life (the beauty of the one and the deformity of the other) than in this book; nor the inviolable rule of God's judgment more plainly laid down, That <hi type="italic">happy are the righteous, it shall be well with them;</hi> and <hi type="italic">Woe to the wicked, it shall be ill with them.</hi> These are not questions of the schools to keep the learned world in action, nor engines of state to keep the unlearned world in awe; no, it appears by this book that they are sacred truths of undoubted certainty, and which all the wise and sober part of mankind have in every age subscribed and submitted to. (2.) It presents us with <hi type="italic">a specimen of Gentile piety.</hi> This great saint descended probably not from Abraham, but Nahor; or, if from Abraham, not from Isaac, but from one of the sons of the concubines that were sent into the east-country (<reference osisRef="Gen.25.6">Gen. xxv. 6</reference>); or, if from Isaac, yet not from Jacob, but Esau; so that he was out of the pale of the covenant of peculiarity, no Israelite, no proselyte, and yet none like him for religion, nor such a favourite of heaven upon this earth. It was a truth therefore, before St. Peter perceived it, that <hi type="italic">in every nation he that fears God and works righteousness is accepted of him,</hi> <reference osisRef="Acts.10.35">Acts x. 35</reference>. There were <hi type="italic">children of God scattered abroad</hi> (<reference osisRef="John.11.52">John xi. 52</reference>) besides the incorporated <hi type="italic">children of the kingdom,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.8.11-Matt.8.12">Matt. viii. 11, 12</reference>. (3.) It presents us with <hi type="italic">an exposition of the book of Providence,</hi> and a clear and satisfactory solution of many of the difficult and obscure passages of it. The prosperity of the wicked and the afflictions of the righteous have always been reckoned two as hard chapters as any in that book; but they are here expounded, and reconciled with the divine wisdom, purity, and goodness, by the <hi type="italic">end of these things.</hi> (4.) It presents us with <hi type="italic">a great example of patience</hi> and close adherence to God in the midst of the sorest calamities. Sir Richard Blackmore's most ingenious pen, in his excellent preface to his paraphrase on this book, makes Job a hero proper for an epic poem; for, says he, "He appears brave in distress and valiant in affliction, maintains his virtue, and with that his character, under the most exasperating provocations that the malice of hell could invent, and thereby gives a most noble example of passive fortitude, a character no way inferior to that of the active hero," &c. (5.) It presents us with <hi type="italic">an illustrious type of Christ,</hi> the particulars of which we shall endeavour to take notice of as we go along. In general, Job was a great sufferer, was emptied and humbled, but in order to his greater glory. So Christ abased himself, that we might be exalted. The learned bishop Patrick quotes St. Jerome more than once speaking of Job as a type of Christ, who <hi type="italic">for the job that was set before him endured the cross,</hi> who was persecuted, for a time, by men and devils, and seemed forsaken of God too, but was raised to be an intercessor even for his friends and had added affliction to his misery. When the apostle speaks of the <hi type="italic">patience of Job</hi> he immediately takes notice of <hi type="italic">the end of the Lord,</hi> that is, of the Lord Jesus (as some understand it), typified by Job, <reference osisRef="Jas.5.11">James v. 11</reference>. <div eID="gen9150" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9151" type="x-p"/> 2. In this book we have, (1.) The history of Job's sufferings, and his patience under them (<reference osisRef="Job.1.1-Job.2.13">ch. i., ii.</reference>, not without a mixture of human frailty, <reference osisRef="Job.3.1-Job.3.26">ch. iii.</reference> (2.) A dispute between him and his friends upon them, in which, [1.] The opponents were Eliphaz, Bildad, and Zophar. [2.] The respondent was Job. [3.] The moderators were, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> Elihu, <reference osisRef="Job.32.1-Job.37.24">ch. xxxii.-xxxvii.</reference> <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> God himself, <reference osisRef="Job.38.1-Job.41.34">ch. xxxviii.-xli.</reference> (3.) The issue of all in Job's honour and prosperity, <reference osisRef="Job.42.1-Job.42.17">ch. xlii.</reference> Upon the whole, we learn that <hi type="italic">many are the afflictions of the righteous, but</hi> that when the Lord <hi type="italic">delivers them out of them all</hi> the <hi type="italic">trial of their faith will be found to praise, and honour, and glory.</hi> <div eID="gen9151" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9152" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen9153" type="x-p"/> The history of Job begins here with an account, I. Of his great piety in general (<reference osisRef="Job.1.1">ver. 1</reference>), and in a particular instance, <reference osisRef="Job.1.5">ver. 5</reference>. II. Of his great prosperity, <reference osisRef="Job.1.2-Job.1.4">ver. 2-4</reference>. III. Of the malice of Satan against him, and the permission he obtained to try his constancy, <reference osisRef="Job.1.6-Job.1.12">ver. 6-12</reference>. IV. Of the surprising troubles that befel him, the ruin of his estate (<reference osisRef="Job.1.13-Job.1.17">ver. 13-17</reference>), and the death of his children, <reference osisRef="Job.1.18-Job.1.19">ver. 18, 19</reference>. V. Of his exemplary patience and piety under these troubles, <reference osisRef="Job.1.20-Job.1.22">ver. 20-22</reference>. In all this he is set forth for an example of suffering affliction, from which no prosperity can secure us, but through which integrity and uprightness will preserve us. <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv24"/> <div eID="gen9153" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen9152" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Job's Character and Possessions. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1520.)</title> <div sID="gen9154" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> There was a man in the land of Uz, whose name <hi type="italic">was</hi> Job; and that man was perfect and upright, and one that feared God, and eschewed evil. <hi type="super">2</hi> And there were born unto him seven sons and three daughters. <hi type="super">3</hi> His substance also was seven thousand sheep, and three thousand camels, and five hundred yoke of oxen, and five hundred she asses, and a very great household; so that this man was the greatest of all the men of the east. <div eID="gen9154" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9155" type="x-p"/> Concerning Job we are here told, <div eID="gen9155" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9156" type="x-p"/> I. That he was a man; therefore subject to like passions as we are. He was <hi type="italic">Ish,</hi> a worthy man, a man of note and eminency, a magistrate, a man in authority. The country he lived in was the land of Uz, in the eastern part of Arabia, which lay towards Chaldea, near Euphrates, probably not far from Ur of the Chaldees, whence Abraham was called. When God called one good man out of that country, yet he <hi type="italic">left not himself without witness,</hi> but raised up another in it to be a <hi type="italic">preacher of righteousness.</hi> God has his remnant in all places, sealed ones out of every nation, as well as out of every tribe of Israel, <reference osisRef="Rev.7.9">Rev. vii. 9</reference>. It was the privilege of the land of Uz to have so good a man as Job in it; now it was <hi type="italic">Arabia the Happy</hi> indeed: and it was the praise of Job that he was eminently good in so bad a place; the worse others were round about him the better he was. His name <hi type="italic">Job,</hi> or <hi type="italic">Jjob,</hi> some say, signifies <hi type="italic">one hated</hi> and counted as an enemy. Others make it to signify one that grieves or groans; thus the sorrow he carried in his name might be a check to his joy in his prosperity. Dr. Cave derives it from <hi type="italic">Jaab—to love,</hi> or <hi type="italic">desire,</hi> intimating how welcome his birth was to his parents, and how much he was <hi type="italic">the desire of their eyes;</hi> and yet there was a time when he cursed the day of his birth. Who can tell what the day may prove which yet begins with a bright morning? <div eID="gen9156" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9157" type="x-p"/> II. That he was a very good man, eminently pious, and better than his neighbours: <hi type="italic">He was perfect and upright.</hi> This is intended to show us, not only what reputation he had among men (that he was generally taken for an honest man), but what was really his character; for it is the judgment of God concerning him, and we are sure that is according to truth. 1. Job was a religious man, <hi type="italic">one that feared God,</hi> that is, worshipped him according to his will, and governed himself by the rules of the divine law in every thing. 2. He was sincere in his religion: He was <hi type="italic">perfect;</hi> not sinless, as he himself owns (<reference osisRef="Job.9.20">ch. ix. 20</reference>): <hi type="italic">If I say I am perfect, I shall be proved perverse.</hi> But, having a respect to all God's commandments, aiming at perfection, he was really as good as he seemed to be, and did not dissemble in his profession of piety; his heart was sound and his eye single. Sincerity is gospel perfection. I know no religion without it. 3. He was upright in his dealings both with God and man, was faithful to his promises, steady in his counsels, true to every trust reposed in him, and made conscience of all he said and did. See <reference osisRef="Isa.33.15">Isa. xxxiii. 15</reference>. Though he was not <hi type="italic">of</hi> Israel, he was indeed an <hi type="italic">Israelite without guile.</hi> 4. The fear of God reigning in his heart was the principle that governed his whole conversation. This made him perfect and upright, inward and entire for God, universal and uniform in religion; this kept him close and constant to his duty. He <hi type="italic">feared God,</hi> had a reverence for his majesty, a regard to his authority, and a dread of his wrath. 5. He dreaded the thought of doing what was wrong; with the utmost abhorrence and detestation, and with a constant care and watchfulness, he <hi type="italic">eschewed evil,</hi> avoided all appearances of sin and approaches to it, and this <hi type="italic">because of the fear of God,</hi> <reference osisRef="Neh.5.15">Neh. v. 15</reference>. <hi type="italic">The fear of the Lord is to hate evil</hi> (<reference osisRef="Prov.8.13">Prov. viii. 13</reference>) and then <hi type="italic">by the fear of the Lord men depart from evil,</hi> <reference osisRef="Prov.16.6">Prov. xvi. 6</reference>. <div eID="gen9157" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9158" type="x-p"/> III. That he was a man who prospered greatly in this world, and made a considerable figure in his country. He was prosperous and yet pious. Though it is hard and rare, it is not impossible, for <hi type="italic">a rich man to enter into the kingdom of heaven.</hi> With God even this is possible, and by his grace the temptations of worldly wealth are not insuperable. He was pious, and his piety was a friend to his prosperity; for godliness has the promise of the life that now is. He was prosperous, and his prosperity put a lustre upon his piety, and gave him who was so good so much greater opportunity of doing good. The acts of his piety were grateful returns to God for the instances of his prosperity; and, in the abundance of the good things God gave him, he served God the more cheerfully. 1. He had a numerous family. He was eminent for religion, and yet not a hermit, not a recluse, but the father and master of a family. It was an instance of his prosperity that his house was filled with children, which are a <hi type="italic">heritage of the Lord,</hi> and his <hi type="italic">reward,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.127.3">Ps. cxxvii. 3</reference>. He had <hi type="italic">seven sons and three daughters,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.1.2">v. 2</reference>. Some of each sex, and more of the more noble sex, in which the family is built up. Children must be looked upon as blessings, for so they are, especially to good people, that will give them good instructions, and set them good examples, and put up good prayers for them. Job had many children, and yet he was neither oppressive nor uncharitable, but very liberal to the poor, <reference osisRef="Job.31.17-Job.31.21">ch. xxxi. 17</reference>, &c. Those that have great families to provide for ought to consider that what is prudently given in alms is set out to the best interest and put into the best fund for their children's benefit. 2. He had a good estate for the support of his family; his <hi type="italic">substance</hi> was considerable, <reference osisRef="Job.1.3">v. 3</reference>. Riches are called <hi type="italic">substance,</hi> in conformity to the common form of speaking; otherwise, to the soul and another world, they are but shadows, <hi type="italic">things that are not,</hi> <reference osisRef="Prov.23.5">Prov. xxiii. 5</reference>. It is only in heavenly wisdom that we <hi type="italic">inherit substance,</hi> <reference osisRef="Prov.8.21">Prov. viii. 21</reference>. In those days, when the earth was not fully peopled, it was as now in some of the plantations, men might have land enough upon easy terms if they had but wherewithal to stock it; and therefore Job's substance is described, not by the acres of land he was lord of, but, (1.) By his cattle—<hi type="italic">sheep and camels, oxen and asses.</hi> The numbers of each are here set down, probably not the exact number, but thereabout, a very few under or over. The sheep are put first, because of most use in the family, as Solomon observes (<reference osisRef="Prov.27.23">Prov. xxvii. 23</reference>, <reference osisRef="Prov.27.26">26</reference>, <reference osisRef="Prov.27.27">27</reference>): <hi type="italic">Lambs for thy clothing, and milk for the food of thy household.</hi> Job, it is likely, had silver and gold as well as Abraham (<reference osisRef="Gen.13.2">Gen. xiii. 2</reference>); but then men valued their own and their neighbours' estates by that which was for service and present use more than by that which was for show and state, and fit only to be hoarded. As soon as God had made man, and provided for his maintenance by the herbs and fruits, he made him rich and great by giving him <hi type="italic">dominion over the creatures,</hi> <reference osisRef="Gen.1.28">Gen. i. 28</reference>. That therefore being still continued to man, notwithstanding his defection (<reference osisRef="Gen.9.2">Gen. ix. 2</reference>), is still to be reckoned one of the most considerable instances of men's wealth, honour, and power, <reference osisRef="Ps.8.6">Ps. viii. 6</reference>. (2.) By his servants. He had a very good household or husbandry, many that were employed for him and maintained by him; and thus he both had honour and did good; yet thus he was involved in a great deal of care and put to a great deal of charge. See the vanity of this world; as goods are increased those must be increased that tend them and occupy them, and <hi type="italic">those will be increased that eat them; and what good has the owner thereof save the beholding of them with his eyes?</hi> <reference osisRef="Eccl.5.11">Eccles. v. 11</reference>. In a word, <hi type="italic">Job was the greatest of all the men of the east;</hi> and they were the richest in the world: those were rich indeed who were <hi type="italic">replenished more than the east,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.2.6">Isa. ii. 6</reference>. Margin. Job's wealth, with his wisdom, entitled him to the honour and power he had in his country, which he describes (<reference osisRef="Job.29.1-Job.29.25">ch. xxix.</reference>), and made him sit chief. Job was upright and honest, and yet grew rich, nay, <hi type="italic">therefore</hi> grew rich; for honesty is the best policy, and piety and charity are ordinarily the surest ways of thriving. He had a great household and much business, and yet kept up the fear and worship of God; and he and his house served the Lord. The account of Job's piety and prosperity comes before the history of his great afflictions, to show that neither will secure us from the common, no, nor from the uncommon calamities of human life. Piety will not secure us, as Job's mistaken friends thought, for <hi type="italic">all things come alike to all;</hi> prosperity will not, as a careless world thinks, <reference osisRef="Isa.47.8">Isa. xlvii. 8</reference>. I sit <hi type="italic">as a queen</hi> and therefore shall <hi type="italic">see no sorrow.</hi>
entries.d5ace0e6e5aa389c085c4e79acaf13faae4f9997: <div eID="gen9158" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Job's Solicitude for His Children. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1520.)</title> <div sID="gen9159" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">4</hi> And his sons went and feasted <hi type="italic">in their</hi> houses, every one his day; and sent and called for their three sisters to eat and to drink with them. <hi type="super">5</hi> And it was so, when the days of <hi type="italic">their</hi> feasting were gone about, that Job sent and sanctified them, and rose up early in the morning, and offered burnt offerings <hi type="italic">according</hi> to the number of them all: for Job said, It may be that my sons have sinned, and cursed God in their hearts. Thus did Job continually. <div eID="gen9159" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9160" type="x-p"/> We have here a further account of Job's prosperity and his piety. <div eID="gen9160" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9161" type="x-p"/> I. His great comfort in his children is taken notice of as an instance of his prosperity; for our temporal comforts are borrowed, depend upon others, and are as those about us are. Job himself mentions it as one of the greatest joys of his prosperous estate that his <hi type="italic">children were about him,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.29.5">ch. xxix. 5</reference>. They kept a circular feast at some certain times (<reference osisRef="Job.1.4">v. 4</reference>); they <hi type="italic">went and feasted in their houses.</hi> It was a comfort to this good man, 1. To see his children grown up and settled in the world. All his sons were in houses of their own, probably married, and to each of them he had given a competent portion to set up with. Those that had been olive-plants round his table were removed to tables of their own. 2. To see them thrive in their affairs, and able to feast one another, as well as to feed themselves. Good parents desire, promote, and rejoice in, their children's wealth and prosperity as their own. 3. To see them in health, no sickness in their houses, for that would have spoiled their feasting and turned it into mourning. 4. Especially to see them live in love, and unity, and mutual good affection, no jars or quarrels among them, no strangeness, no shyness one of another, no strait-handedness, but, though every one knew his own, they lived with as much freedom as if they had had all in common. It is comfortable to the hearts of parents, and comely in the eyes of all, to see brethren thus knit together. <hi type="italic">Behold, how good and how pleasant it is!</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.133.1">Ps. cxxxiii. 1</reference>. 5. It added to his comfort to see the brothers so kind to their sisters, that they sent for them to feast with them; for they were so modest that they would not have gone if they had not been sent for. Those brothers that slight their sisters, care not for their company, and have no concern for their comfort, are ill-bred, ill-natured, and very unlike Job's sons. It seems their feast was so sober and decent that their sisters were good company for them at it. 6. They feasted in their own houses, not in public houses, where they would be more exposed to temptations, and which were not so creditable. We do not find that Job himself feasted with them. Doubtless they invited him, and he would have been the most welcome guest at any of their tables; nor was it from any sourness or moroseness of temper, or for want of natural affection, that he kept away, but he was old and dead to these things, like Barzillai (<reference osisRef="2Sam.19.35">2 Sam. xix. 35</reference>), and considered that the young people would be more free and pleasant if there were none but themselves. Yet he would not restrain his children from that diversion which he denied himself. Young people may be allowed a youthful liberty, provided they flee youthful lusts. <div eID="gen9161" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9162" type="x-p"/> II. His great care about his children is taken notice of as an instance of his piety: for that we are really which we are relatively. Those that are good will be good to their children, and especially do what they can for the good of their souls. Observe (<reference osisRef="Job.1.5">v. 5</reference>) Job's pious concern for the spiritual welfare of his children, <div eID="gen9162" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9163" type="x-p"/> 1. He was jealous over them with a godly jealousy; and so we ought to be over ourselves and those that are dearest to us, as far as is necessary to our care and endeavour for their good. Job had given his children a good education, had comfort in them and good hope concerning them; and yet he said, "<hi type="italic">It may be, my sons have sinned</hi> in the days of their feasting more than at other times, have been too merry, have taken too great a liberty in eating and drinking, and have <hi type="italic">cursed God in their hearts,</hi>" that is, "have entertained atheistical or profane thoughts in their minds, unworthy notions of God and his providence, and the exercises of religion." When they were <hi type="italic">full</hi> they were ready to <hi type="italic">deny God, and to say, Who is the Lord?</hi> (<reference osisRef="Prov.30.9">Prov. xxx. 9</reference>), ready to <hi type="italic">forget</hi> God and to say, The <hi type="italic">power of our hand</hi> has <hi type="italic">gotten us this wealth,</hi> <reference osisRef="Deut.8.12-Deut.8.17">Deut. viii. 12</reference>, &c. Nothing alienates the mind more from God than the indulgence of the flesh. <div eID="gen9163" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9164" type="x-p"/> 2. As soon as the days of their feasting were over he called them to the solemn exercises of religion. Not while their feasting lasted (let them take their time for that; there is a time for all things), but when it was over, their good father reminded them that they must know when to desist, and not think to fare sumptuously every day; though they had their days of feasting the <hi type="italic">week</hi> round, they must not think to have them the <hi type="italic">year</hi> round; they had something else to do. Note, Those that are merry must find a time to be serious. <div eID="gen9164" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9165" type="x-p"/> 3. He sent to them to prepare for solemn ordinances, <hi type="italic">sent and sanctified them,</hi> ordered them to examine their own consciences and repent of what they had done amiss in their feasting, to lay aside their vanity and compose themselves for religious exercises. Thus he kept his authority over them for their good, and they submitted to it, though they had got into houses of their own. Still he was the priest of the family, and at his altar they all attended, valuing their share in his prayers more than their share in his estate. Parents cannot give grace to their children (it is God that sanctifies), but they ought by seasonable admonitions and counsels to further their sanctification. In their baptism they were sanctified to God; let it be our desire and endeavour that they may be sanctified for him. <div eID="gen9165" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9166" type="x-p"/> 4. He offered sacrifice for them, both to atone for the sins he feared they had been guilty of in the days of their feasting and to implore for them mercy to pardon and grace to prevent the debauching of their minds and corrupting of their manners by the liberty they had taken, and to preserve their piety and purity. <div eID="gen9166" type="x-p"/> <lg sID="gen9167"/> <l level="1" sID="gen9168"/>For he with mournful eyes had often spied,<l eID="gen9168" level="1"/> <l level="1" sID="gen9169"/>Scattered on Pleasure's smooth but treacherous tide,<l eID="gen9169" level="1"/> <l level="1" sID="gen9170"/>The spoils of virtue overpowered by sense,<l eID="gen9170" level="1"/> <l level="1" sID="gen9171"/>And floating wrecks of ruined innocence. Sir <hi type="small-caps">R. Blackmore</hi> .<l eID="gen9171" level="1"/> <lg eID="gen9167"/> <div sID="gen9172" type="x-p"/> Job, like Abraham, had an altar for his family, on which, it is likely, he offered sacrifice daily; but, on this extraordinary occasion, he offered more sacrifices than usual, and with more solemnity, <hi type="italic">according to the number of them all,</hi> one for each child. Parents should be particular in their addresses to God for the several branches of their family. "For this child I prayed, according to its particular temper, genius, and condition," to which the prayers, as well as the endeavours, must be accommodated. When these sacrifices were to be offered, (1.) He rose early, as one in care that his children might not lie long under guilt and as one whose heart was upon his work and his desire towards it. (2.) He required his children to attend the sacrifice, that they might join with him in the prayers he offered with the sacrifice, that the sight of the killing of the sacrifice might humble them much for their sins, for which they deserved to die, and the sight of the offering of it up might lead them to a Mediator. This serious work would help to make them serious again after the days of their gaiety. <div eID="gen9172" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9173" type="x-p"/> 5. Thus he did <hi type="italic">continually,</hi> and not merely whenever an occasion of this kind recurred; for <hi type="italic">he that is washed needs to wash his feet,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.13.10">John xiii. 10</reference>. The acts of repentance and faith must be often renewed, because we often repeat our transgressions. All days, every day, he offered up his sacrifices, was constant to his devotions, and did not omit them any day. The occasional exercises of religion will not excuse us from those that are stated. He that serves God uprightly will serve him continually.
entries.8a177afa45866a9ccf586185a3c8c7e8fca6dddf: <div eID="gen9173" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Satan before God; Satan Permitted to Afflict Job. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1520.)</title> <div sID="gen9174" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">6</hi> Now there was a day when the sons of God came to present themselves before the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , and Satan came also among them. <hi type="super">7</hi> And the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> said unto Satan, Whence comest thou? Then Satan answered the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , and said, From going to and fro in the earth, and from walking up and down in it. <hi type="super">8</hi> And the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> said unto Satan, Hast thou considered my servant Job, that <hi type="italic">there is</hi> none like him in the earth, a perfect and an upright man, one that feareth God, and escheweth evil? <hi type="super">9</hi> Then Satan answered the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , and said, Doth Job fear God for nought? 10 Hast not thou made a hedge about him, and about his house, and about all that he hath on every side? thou hast blessed the work of his hands, and his substance is increased in the land. 11 But put forth thine hand now, and touch all that he hath, and he will curse thee to thy face. <hi type="super">12</hi> And the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> said unto Satan, Behold, all that he hath <hi type="italic">is</hi> in thy power; only upon himself put not forth thine hand. So Satan went forth from the presence of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <div eID="gen9174" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9175" type="x-p"/> Job was not only so rich and great, but withal so wise and good, and had such an interest both in heaven and earth, that one would think the mountain of his prosperity stood so strong that it could not be moved; but here we have a thick cloud gathering over his head, pregnant with a horrible tempest. We must never think ourselves secure from storms while we are in this lower region. Before we are told how his troubles surprised and seized him here in this visible world, we are here told how they were concerted in the world of spirits, that the devil, having a great enmity to Job for his eminent piety, begged and obtained leave to torment him. It does not at all derogate from the credibility of Job's story in general to allow that this discourse between God and Satan, in these verses, is parabolical, like that of Micaiah (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.22.19-1Kgs.22.29">1 Kings xxii. 19</reference>, &c.), and an allegory designed to represent the malice of the devil against good men and the divine check and restraint which that malice is under; only thus much further is intimated, that the affairs of this earth are very much the subject of the counsels of the unseen world. That world is dark to us, but we lie very open to it. Now here we have, <div eID="gen9175" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9176" type="x-p"/> I. Satan among the sons of God (<reference osisRef="Job.1.6">v. 6</reference>), an <hi type="italic">adversary</hi> (so <hi type="italic">Satan</hi> signifies) to God, to men, to all good: he thrust himself into an assembly of the <hi type="italic">sons of God</hi> that came to <hi type="italic">present themselves before the Lord.</hi> This means either, 1. A meeting of the saints on earth. Professors of religion, in the patriarchal age, were called <hi type="italic">sons of God</hi> (<reference osisRef="Gen.6.2">Gen. vi. 2</reference>); they had then religious assemblies and stated times for them. The King came in to see his guests; the eye of God was on all present. But there was a serpent in paradise, a Satan among the sons of God; when they come together he is among them, to distract and disturb them, stands at their right hand to resist them. <hi type="italic">The Lord rebuke thee, Satan!</hi> Or, 2. A meeting of the angels in heaven. They are <hi type="italic">the sons of God,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.38.7">ch. xxxviii. 7</reference>. They came to give an account of their negotiations on earth and to receive new instructions. Satan was one of them originally; but <hi type="italic">how hast thou fallen, O Lucifer!</hi> He shall no more stand in that congregation, yet he is here represented, as coming among them, either summoned to appear as a criminal or connived at, for the present, though an intruder. <div eID="gen9176" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9177" type="x-p"/> II. His examination, how he came thither (<reference osisRef="Job.1.7">v. 7</reference>): <hi type="italic">The Lord said unto Satan, Whence comest thou?</hi> He knew very well whence he came, and with what design he came thither, that as the good angels came to do good he came for a permission to do hurt; but he would, by calling him to an account, show him that he was under check and control. <hi type="italic">Whence comest thou?</hi> He asks this, 1. As wondering what brought him thither. <hi type="italic">Is Saul among the prophets?</hi> Satan among the sons of God? Yes, for he <hi type="italic">transforms himself into an angel of light</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Cor.11.13-2Cor.11.14">2 Cor. xi. 13, 14</reference>), and would seem one of them. Note, It is possible that a man may be a child of the devil and yet be found in the assemblies of the sons of God in this world, and <hi type="italic">there</hi> may pass undiscovered by men, and yet be challenged by the all-seeing God. <hi type="italic">Friend, how camest thou in hither?</hi> Or, 2. As enquiring what he had been doing before he came thither. The same question was perhaps put to the rest of those that presented themselves before the Lord, "Whence came you?" We are accountable to God for all our haunts and all the ways we traverse. <div eID="gen9177" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9178" type="x-p"/> III. The account he gives of himself and of the tour he had made. I come (says he) <hi type="italic">from going to and fro on the earth.</hi> 1. He could not pretend he had been doing any good, could give no such account of himself as the sons of God could, who <hi type="italic">presented themselves before the Lord,</hi> who came from executing his orders, serving the interest of his kingdom, and ministering to the heirs of salvation. 2. He would not own he had been doing any hurt, that he had been drawing men from the allegiance to God, deceiving and destroying souls; no. <hi type="italic">I have done no wickedness,</hi> <reference osisRef="Prov.30.20">Prov. xxx. 20</reference>. <hi type="italic">Thy servant went nowhere.</hi> In saying that he had <hi type="italic">walked to and fro through the earth,</hi> he intimates that he had kept himself within the bounds allotted him, and had not transgressed his bounds; for <hi type="italic">the dragon is cast out into the earth</hi> (<reference osisRef="Rev.12.9">Rev. xii. 9</reference>) and not yet confined to his place of torment. While we are on this earth we are within his reach, and with so much subtlety, swiftness, and industry, does he penetrate into all the corners of it, that we cannot be in any place secure from his temptations. 3. He yet seems to give some representation of his own character. (1.) Perhaps it is spoken proudly, and with an air of haughtiness, as if he were indeed the <hi type="italic">prince of this world,</hi> as if <hi type="italic">the kingdoms of the world and the glory of them</hi> were his (<reference osisRef="Luke.4.6">Luke iv. 6</reference>), and he had now been walking in circuit through his own territories. (2.) Perhaps it is spoken fretfully, and with discontent. He had been walking to and fro, and could find no rest, but was as much a fugitive and a vagabond as Cain in the land of Nod. (3.) Perhaps it is spoken carefully: "I have been hard at work, going to and fro," or (as some read it) "searching about in the earth," really in quest of an opportunity to do mischief. He walks abut seeking whom he may devour. It concerns us therefore to be sober and vigilant. <div eID="gen9178" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9179" type="x-p"/> IV. The question God puts to him concerning Job (<reference osisRef="Job.1.8">v. 8</reference>): <hi type="italic">Hast thou considered my servant Job?</hi> As when we meet with one that has been in a distant place, where we have a friend we dearly love, we are ready to ask, "You have been in such a place; pray did you see my friend there?" Observe, 1. How honourably God speaks of Job: He is <hi type="italic">my servant.</hi> Good men are God's servants, and he is pleased to reckon himself honoured in their services, and they are to him for <hi type="italic">a name and a praise</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jer.13.11">Jer. xiii. 11</reference>) <hi type="italic">and a crown of glory,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.62.3">Isa. lxii. 3</reference>. "Yonder is <hi type="italic">my servant Job;</hi> there is <hi type="italic">none like him,</hi> none I value like him, of all the princes and potentates of the earth; one such saint as he is worth them all: <hi type="italic">none like him</hi> for uprightness and serious piety; many do well, but <hi type="italic">he excelleth them all;</hi> there is not to be found <hi type="italic">such great faith, no, not in Israel.</hi>" Thus Christ, long after, commended the centurion and the woman of Canaan, who were both of them, like Job, strangers to that commonwealth. The saints glory in God—<hi type="italic">Who is like thee among the gods?</hi> and he is pleased to glory in them—<hi type="italic">Who is like Israel among the people?</hi> So here, <hi type="italic">none like Job,</hi> none in earth, that state of imperfection. Those in heaven do indeed far outshine him; those who are least in that kingdom are greater than he; but <hi type="italic">on earth there is not his like.</hi> There is none like him in that land; so some good men are the glory of their country. 2. How closely he gives to Satan this good character of Job: <hi type="italic">Hast thou set thy heart to my servant Job?</hi> designing hereby, (1.) To aggravate the apostasy and misery of that wicked spirit: "How unlike him are thou!" Note, The holiness and happiness of the saints are the shame and torment of the devil and the devil's children. (2.) To answer the devil's seeming boast of the interest he had in this earth. "I have been walking to and fro in it," says he, "and it is all my own; all flesh have corrupted their way; they all sit still, and are at rest in their sins," <reference osisRef="Zech.1.10-Zech.1.11">Zech. i. 10, 11</reference>. "Nay, hold," saith God, "Job is my faithful servant." Satan may boast, but he shall not triumph. (3.) To anticipate his accusations, as if he had said, "Satan, I know thy errand; thou hast come to inform against Job; but <hi type="italic">hast thou considered him?</hi> Does not his unquestionable character give thee the lie?" Note, God knows all the malice of the devil and his instruments against his servants; and we have an advocate ready to appear for us, even before we are accused. <div eID="gen9179" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9180" type="x-p"/> V. The devil's base insinuation against Job, in answer to God's encomium of him. He could not deny but that Job feared God, but suggested that he was a mercenary in his religion, and therefore a hypocrite (<reference osisRef="Job.1.9">v. 9</reference>): <hi type="italic">Doth Job fear God for nought?</hi> Observe, 1. How impatient the devil was of hearing Job praised, though it was God himself that praised him. Those are like the devil who cannot endure that any body should be praised but themselves, but grudge the just share of reputation others have, as Saul (<reference osisRef="1Sam.18.5-1Sam.18.16">1 Sam. xviii. 5</reference>, &c.) and the Pharisees, <reference osisRef="Matt.21.15">Matt. xxi. 15</reference>. 2. How much at a loss he was for something to object against him; he could not accuse him of any thing that was bad, and therefore charged him with by-ends in doing good. Had the one half of that been true which his angry friends, in the heat of dispute, charged him with (<reference osisRef="Job.15.4">ch. xv. 4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Job.22.5">xxii. 5</reference>), Satan would no doubt have brought against him now; but no such thing could be alleged, and therefore, 3. See how slyly he censured him as a hypocrite, not asserting that he was so, but only asking, "Is he not so?" This is the common way of slanderers, whisperers, backbiters, to suggest that by way of query which yet they have no reason to think is true. Note, It is not strange if those that are approved and accepted of God be unjustly censured by the devil and his instruments; if they are otherwise unexceptionable, it is easy to charge them with hypocrisy, as Satan charged Job, and they have no way to clear themselves, but patiently to wait for the judgment of God. As there is nothing we should dread more than being hypocrites, so there is nothing we need dread less that being called and counted so without cause. 4. How unjustly he accused him as mercenary, to prove him a hypocrite. It was a great truth that Job did not fear God for nought; he got much by it, for godliness is great gain: but it was a falsehood that he would not have feared God if he had not got this by it, as the event proved. Job's friends charged him with hypocrisy because he was greatly afflicted, Satan because he greatly prospered. It is no hard matter for those to calumniate that seek an occasion. It is not mercenary to look at the eternal recompence in our obedience; but to aim at temporal advantages in our religion, and to make it subservient to them, is spiritual idolatry, worshipping the creature more than the Creator, and is likely to end in a fatal apostasy. Men cannot long <hi type="italic">serve God and mammon.</hi> <div eID="gen9180" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9181" type="x-p"/> VI. The complaint Satan made of Job's prosperity, <reference osisRef="Job.1.10">v. 10</reference>. Observe, 1. What God had done for Job. He had protected him, made a hedge about him, for the defence of his person, his family, and all his possessions. Note, God's peculiar people are taken under his special protection, they and all that belong to them; divine grace makes a hedge about their spiritual life, and divine providence about their natural life, so they are safe and easy. He had prospered him, not in idleness or injustice (the devil could not accuse him of them), but in the way of honest diligence: <hi type="italic">Thou hast blessed the work of his hands.</hi> Without that blessing, be the hands ever so strong, ever so skilful, the work will not prosper; but, with that, <hi type="italic">his substance has wonderfully increased in the land.</hi> The blessing of the Lord makes rich: Satan himself owns it. 2. What notice the devil took of it, and how he improved it against him. The devil speaks of it with vexation.
